docs.title: FPGA from Scratch -- Under Development
docs.text:
An open-toolchain book on FPGA design. It starts from what an FPGA is and builds, step by step, a complete high-frequency-trading data path (Ethernet, UDP and TCP, exchange market data, an order book, triggers, pre-trade risk and order entry) as the main running case study; it then applies the same method to case studies in signal processing, radio, security, compression, control, vision, genomics, finance and machine learning.

Status

The book is under development. This site currently holds the plan: see Contents for every part and chapter, what each will build, and the tests it will carry. Chapters are added one at a time, each with its code, its recorded output and its mutation run.

docs.title: The method (the same as in Capra: Silicon Compiler from Scratch)
docs.text:
• an independent Python golden model for every circuit;
  • self-checking testbenches in two simulators (Icarus Verilog and Verilator);
  • every test is tested: break the design one line at a time and check that the tests notice (mutation testing); equivalent mutants are listed apart from real gaps;
  • every number is labelled measured, derived or assumed;
  • "a model of a design, not a product": no claim goes beyond what the open tools can show.

docs.title: What this book is not
docs.text:
It uses open tools only (Yosys, nextpnr, Verilator, Icarus Verilog, SymbiYosys). It does not use Vivado, a board, a real 10G PHY or a live exchange feed, so latency is reported in cycles at a stated clock, never as measured wire-to-wire nanoseconds, and risk logic is presented as an educational design, not as certified compliance logic.

Companion books: Capra: Silicon Compiler from Scratch and the OS-from-scratch book.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: The plan for the whole book. Part 0 to Part 7 build the trading data path; Parts 8 to 11 are case studies from other domains. Every chapter carries two running examples, figures, a Python golden model, tests in two simulators, a mutation run and self-check questions with answers (Appendix H). Status: all chapters are planned.

docs.title: Part 1 -- Foundations
docs.text:
1. What an FPGA is: LUTs, flip-flops, carry chains, block RAM, DSP slices, clocks, I/O, and the open flow used here
  2. Hardware design in SystemVerilog: the synthesizable subset, packages, structs, interfaces, FSM style, linting
  3. Timing: clocks, setup and hold, reset strategy, clock-domain crossing, reading a timing report
  4. Latency as a budget: pipelines, valid/ready, cut-through against store-and-forward, determinism
  5. Resources: LUT against DSP against BRAM, fixed-point arithmetic, retiming, what actually costs area
  6. A verification harness: Verilator drivers, Python golden models, vector replay, constrained random, mutation testing, formal properties

docs.title: Part 2 -- Wire to bytes: Ethernet
docs.text:
1. Frames and the CRC: parallel CRC-32 at 64 bits per beat
  2. The MAC datapath: AXI-Stream, FIFOs, clock crossing, the PHY modeled at its interface
  3. VLAN, IPv4 and UDP at line rate: parsing across beat boundaries, checksums, drop rules
  4. Filtering: address and port matching, hash filters, small CAMs, multicast groups
  5. Egress: frame building, padding, checksums, pacing

docs.title: Part 3 -- Reliable transport: TCP
docs.text:
1. Why orders use TCP: the state machine and what must be in hardware
  2. A TCP offload engine: sequence and ack tracking, retransmit timers, windows
  3. Testing it against a deterministic reference stack with loss, reorder and duplication injected; formal safety properties
  4. Hot path and cold path: reconnects, head-of-line blocking, the hardware/software split

docs.title: Part 4 -- Market data
docs.text:
1. Exchange protocols: MoldUDP64, ITCH, SoupBinTCP and OUCH, and a generator that turns a message grammar into a parser
  2. Line-rate message parsing: variable-length messages across beats, several messages per packet
  3. Sequence gaps and A/B feed arbitration
  4. The order book in hardware: per-symbol state, price-level structures (sorted array, CAM, hash in BRAM), top of book
  5. Order-book engineering: worst-case latency against depth, checked against a Python golden book

docs.title: Part 5 -- Decide and act
docs.text:
1. Triggers: predicates on messages, pipelined comparators, symbol tables
  2. Fixed-point signals: imbalance, mid and microprice on DSP and LUT
  3. Pre-trade risk: position, notional and rate limits, price bands, kill switch, fail-closed design, formal proof of the invariants
  4. Order entry: binary encoding, pre-built templates, session state, sequence numbers
  5. Order lifecycle: acks, cancels, replaces, fills, reconciliation

docs.title: Part 6 -- The whole system
docs.text:
1. Integration: the wire-to-wire pipeline, a per-stage cycle-budget table, a register interface and DMA to the host
  2. Resets, power-up, watchdogs and safe states
  3. Timestamps and measurement: defining tick-to-trade, jitter, histograms
  4. System tests: replay, scenario generation, fault injection, cycle-count regression

docs.title: Part 7 -- Trading case studies and techniques
docs.text:
1. Speculative processing: parse before the checksum clears, with rollback; pre-computed responses
  2. Latency against determinism: where jitter comes from, fixed pipelines against dynamic ones
  3. Hybrid designs: an FPGA filter in front of a CPU book
  4. Many feeds, many venues: arbitration, resource sharing, floorplanning
  5. FPGA, ASIC or CPU: a cost model for deciding what belongs in hardware
  6. Operations and audit: logging, kill-switch drills, change control (as education, not compliance logic)

docs.title: Part 8 -- Case studies: signals and radio
docs.text:
1. A polyphase channelizer and FFT pipeline: streaming fixed-point FFT, an SNR study against a floating-point reference
  2. A software-defined-radio receiver: digital downconverter, CORDIC mixer, symbol timing recovery, a Viterbi or LDPC decoder checked against a bit-error-rate curve

docs.title: Part 9 -- Case studies: security and data infrastructure
docs.text:
1. A TLS record engine: AES-GCM in hardware, NIST test vectors as golden data
  2. SHA-256 and a Merkle-tree offload
  3. A compression engine: LZ77 matching and Huffman coding, round-tripped against zlib
  4. A regex and deep-packet-inspection engine: regex to DFA in hardware, checked against Python's re
  5. A key-value store accelerator: a hash table in BRAM with an LSM-style write path

docs.title: Part 10 -- Case studies: control and vision
docs.text:
1. A motor-control loop: fixed-point PID, field-oriented control, ADC timing, a plant model co-simulated
  2. A computer-vision pipeline: line buffers, convolution, Sobel edges, connected components
  3. A real-time 3D transform and rasterizer: barycentric rasterization, a depth buffer, a test image

docs.title: Part 11 -- Case studies: science, finance and machine learning
docs.text:
1. A genomics seed-and-extend aligner: a Smith-Waterman systolic array checked against a Python reference
  2. A Monte-Carlo option pricer: an LFSR and Box-Muller random source, the variance against the analytic price
  3. Neural-network inference: a tiny convolutional network in fixed point, tied back to Capra's quantization chapters
  4. Sparse linear algebra: SpMV and a conjugate-gradient solver, with the memory bottleneck analysed

docs.title: Appendices
docs.text:
• A. Digital logic recap · B. SystemVerilog reference · C. Ethernet, IP and TCP reference · D. Exchange-protocol reference · E. FPGA families and toolchains · F. Timing-closure playbook · G. Verification cookbook · H. Answers to all self-check questions
  • Primers for the case studies: I. DSP · J. Cryptography · K. Error-correcting codes · L. Computer graphics

docs.title: How it will be built
docs.text: In volumes: Volume 1 is Parts 1 to 4, Volume 2 is Parts 5 to 7, Volume 3 is Parts 8 to 11. The chapters of the case-study parts (36 to 49) are independent of each other and can be read in any order after Part 1. Chapters 45 and 46 are marked optional: they are far from the trading path and are included to show the method generalizes.
